# Traffic Monitor

> Open-source roadway counting and speed monitoring on a Raspberry Pi

The Traffic Monitor turns a Raspberry Pi 5 with a camera, Doppler radar, and an optional AI accelerator into an open source roadway counter and speed monitor. These docs cover hardware, installation, setup, configuration, the on-device dashboards, and data payloads.

# Get started

# Traffic Monitor docs

[Traffic Monitor](https://www.trafficmonitor.ai/) is open source software that turns a Raspberry Pi 5 with a camera and a Doppler radar into a roadway counter and speed monitor. It counts pedestrians, bicycles, and vehicles, measures vehicle speeds, and keeps the data on the device.

Be counted

Privacy is part of the design. Object detection runs on the device, the database records labels, speeds, and times rather than people, and nothing is sent to an outside server unless you set it up. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/index.md) lists what the device stores, including the short-lived snapshots and clips that Frigate keeps by default, and who on your network can see them.

Our mission is to democratize the power of AI tools to improve community safety and quality of life, through the ethical and transparent use of these capabilities.

# How it works

A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5 running a few cooperating programs. Everything happens on the device, so it works without an internet connection once it's installed.

## From the street to the database

1. **The camera** streams H.265 video at 1536×864 and 10 frames per second to Frigate.

1. **[Frigate](https://frigate.video/)** finds and tracks objects in the video, using the AI accelerator if the device has one and the CPU if not. It records which **zones** each object passed through. When an object leaves the frame, Frigate publishes an event on the device's MQTT broker.

1. **The radar** (optional) measures the speed and direction of whatever moves in front of it and reports readings over USB several times a second.

1. **[Node-RED](https://nodered.org/)** runs the Traffic Monitor logic. It keeps every radar reading, and it records every moving object from an enabled camera as an event. When the camera has a radar and the object entered any zone, it:

   - works out the direction of travel from the order in which the object entered `zone_near` and `zone_far`, or from the radar if the zones don't give one;
   - attaches a speed: the median radar reading in that direction while the object was in view, with a two-second margin on each side.

   Without a radar, events have no direction or speed. [Direction and speed](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/#direction-and-speed) has the exact rules.

   The dashboards and the daily counts then filter the events by zone: they count objects that passed through `zone_capture`, and they use only objects that passed through `zone_radar` for speed statistics. 5. **The database**, one SQLite file on the device, stores the events, the radar readings, air quality readings from the optional sensor, and the device's deployment history. The dashboards read from it, and you can download it.

[First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md) walks through turning on detection and adjusting the four zones. [Events](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/index.md) lists every column an event has.

## What you see

The device serves a home page at `http://<device>/` that links to the dashboards, Frigate, and the system tools. [Home page and apps](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/home-page/index.md) describes each one.

## What stays on the device

The database holds labels, times, speeds, and zones, not pictures. Frigate keeps cropped snapshots and short clips for about an hour so you can check what was detected, and nothing is sent anywhere unless you turn on an integration. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/index.md) has the details.

## Settings

Three files on the device control the behavior described above. You edit them over SSH.

| File                    | What it controls                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Frigate's `config.yml`  | Camera, detection, zones, object filters, and recording. Most changes are made in Frigate's own web UI. See [Tune object detection](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/index.md).                                                                                            |
| Node-RED's `config.yml` | Deployment location, which sensors are on, which radar pairs with which camera, and the ThingsBoard connection. Times shown on the dashboards use the device's time zone, which the installer sets. See [config.yml settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/index.md). |
| `node-red-tm.env`       | Radar serial ports, the database path, and the MQTT broker. See [node-red-tm.env settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/environment/index.md).                                                                                                                                        |

# Choose your path

## 1. Get a Traffic Monitor

- **[Build your own](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/index.md)**

  ______________________________________________________________________

  Buy the [hardware](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/index.md), [assemble](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/assembly-instructions/index.md) it, and [install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/index.md). The software is open source and the parts are sold at retail.

- **Start with a pre-built unit**

  ______________________________________________________________________

  The software is installed. Skip to step 2, and ask your provider how the unit connects to your network.

## 2. Deploy it

The device needs a clear view of the roadway, and the radar needs a shallow angle to the direction of travel. [Choose a site and mount](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/index.md) covers both, for [temporary](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/#temporary-deployments) and [permanent](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/#permanent-deployments) deployments.

## 3. Set it up

Power it on and follow [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md): open the home page, turn on detection, adjust the zones to your roadway, and record the device's location. This takes about half an hour.

## 4. Use the data

The device counts around the clock and starts again by itself after a power cut. Watch the [Monitoring dashboard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/monitoring/index.md), review detections in Frigate, [export the data](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/database/index.md), or send it to [ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/index.md).

Some operators pair the device with a display that shows the day's counts. Share what you build in [Show and tell](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions/new?category=show-and-tell) or on the [Zulip chat](https://trafficmonitor.zulipchat.com/).

LED display showing daily counts from a Traffic Monitor
# Build your own

# Build your own

A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5, a camera, an optional radar and AI accelerator, and a weather-resistant enclosure. Building one takes an afternoon.

1. [Hardware](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/index.md): the parts list, with the options that have been tested.
1. [Assembly](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/assembly-instructions/index.md): fitting the parts into the 3D-printed enclosure.
1. [Install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/index.md): image the microSD card and run the installer.
1. [Update the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/update/index.md): when a new release comes out.

Then continue with [Choose a site and mount](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/index.md) and [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md).

# Assembly

These steps assume the [parts list](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/index.md) and the 3D-printed enclosure. Each numbered step matches a numbered photo.

Full set of Traffic Monitor parts ready for assembly

Steps 1 to 34 assemble the Raspberry Pi 5, Camera Module 3, AI accelerator (Coral TPU HAT or AI HAT+), and radar. Steps 35 to 51 add the optional air quality sensor.

## Core parts

1. Lay out all your parts and screws
1. Lay out all your parts and screws (double-check)
1. M3×12 mm screws for the camera, M3×6 mm for the radar, M3×10 mm for the carrier board
1. Lay out all your parts and screws
1. (Coral TPU M.2 module and HAT pictured) Unbox the AI accelerator and the M.2 board, if separate
1. (Coral TPU M.2 module and HAT pictured) Attach the M.2 module to the board and attach the ribbon cable
1. Attach the active cooler to the Raspberry Pi
1. Lay out the HAT stand-offs
1. Attach the stand-offs to the board (bottom-HAT version shown)
1. Plug in the PCIe ribbon cable. *Match the triangle marks on the ribbon cable, the Raspberry Pi, and the HAT.*
1. Attach the HAT to the Raspberry Pi (bottom HAT shown, for the Coral TPU)
1. Locate the Raspberry Pi carrier plate
1. Turn the carrier plate so the built-in stand-offs point down
1. Mount the Raspberry Pi and HAT to the carrier plate
1. Bottom of the carrier plate
1. Locate the radar and its mounting board
1. Attach the radar to the mounting board with M3×6 mm screws, with the antenna (the white and gold areas) at the bottom and the micro-USB plug near the camera cut-out
1. Locate the camera, camera mounts, and camera ribbon cable
1. If the camera came with a white ribbon cable, remove it. It doesn't fit the Raspberry Pi 5.
1. Attach the Raspberry Pi 5 camera ribbon cable to the camera
1. Slide the camera into the first camera mounting plate
1. Snap on the other camera mounting plate so all the holes and pins align
1. The camera mount stand-offs are on the back, and the first plate sits flush with the end of the stand-offs
1. Locate the main mounting board and the assembled camera mount
1. Locate four M3×12 mm screws for the camera
1. (Pictures continue below) Mount the camera in either of the camera mount holes
1. Radar and camera mounted, from the front
1. Pass the camera ribbon cable through the camera mounting hole to the back
1. Front view with the camera ribbon cable through the back
1. Locate the main mounting board, the carrier plate, and the M3×10 mm screws
1. Attach the carrier board to the main board
1. Front view with the carrier board attached
1. Plug the camera ribbon cable into either of the Raspberry Pi 5 camera connectors
1. Place the main mounting board into the enclosure, with the radar and camera at the top facing forward, and secure it with M3×10 mm screws in the four corners

## Air quality sensor

35. Locate the Enviro+ board and the particulate matter (PM) sensor
01. Unpack both
01. Attach the Enviro+ board to the PM sensor
01. Back of the Enviro+ board
01. Locate the GPIO ribbon cable
01. Attach the ribbon cable to the Enviro+ board with the wires going down and the notch on top
01. Place the PM sensor in its slot, pushed fully onto the pins in the bottom of the enclosure
01. The PM sensor from below
01. Slip the Enviro+ board into the air quality carrier board
01. Line up the pins on the bottom of the carrier board with the Enviro+ board. It may be snug.
01. Gently place the carrier board into the alignment slots in the enclosure
01. There should be almost no gap between the carrier board and the enclosure
01. Fold the ribbon cable up and tuck the PM sensor cable on top of the PM sensor
01. Slide the air quality shroud into its slots so you can see the screw inserts, and secure it with M3×8 mm screws
01. Front of the assembled sensor
01. Top of the assembled sensor
01. The assembled sensor from outside the enclosure

### Attach the GPIO ribbon cable

Attach the ribbon cable to the Raspberry Pi's GPIO pins with the notch on top.

Attach the ribbon cable with the notch toward the outside of the Raspberry Pi

- Pre-fold the cable so it lies flat when the case is closed.
- The connector is tight on the pins and close to the cooler's heatsink. Work it down a few millimeters at a time, side to side, until it's fully seated.
- To remove it, unplug the Raspberry Pi first. Slide a flat-head screwdriver between the connector and the plastic header and work the connector off a few millimeters at a time, taking care not to short the pins.

## Ready to deploy

Close the case. Next, [install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/index.md).

Traffic Monitors ready to count

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The parts for a Traffic Monitor: Raspberry Pi 5, camera, AI accelerator, radar, enclosure, power, and the optional air quality sensor.

# Hardware

The core parts are the Raspberry Pi 5, a microSD card, a camera, and an AI accelerator. A radar adds accurate speeds, and an air quality sensor adds environmental readings. You can swap parts, but the docs and the default settings assume the parts below.

What each combination gives you:

1. **Camera and AI accelerator**: object detection and counts. The lowest cost.
1. **Add a radar** for speeds and the direction of travel. Without a radar, events have no speed or direction.
1. **Add an air quality sensor** for gases, particulate matter, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light.
1. **Add cameras** to watch more directions with the same accelerator. The software supports several cameras and up to four radars, paired in any pattern. See [Cameras](#cameras).

## Parts list

We are not affiliated with the stores or companies linked here. These are parts contributors have used or tested; if you've tested others, post in the [discussions](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions).

- Computer: [Raspberry Pi 5](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-5/), 4 GB or 8 GB
  - Power: the official [27 W USB-C power supply](https://www.pishop.us/product/raspberry-pi-27w-usb-c-power-supply-black-us/)
  - Cooling: the [Raspberry Pi active cooler](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/active-cooler/)
- Storage: a microSD card of 32 GB or more, such as the [Raspberry Pi SD card](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/sd-cards/) or the [SanDisk Extreme Pro](https://www.westerndigital.com/products/memory-cards/sandisk-extreme-pro-uhs-i-microsd?sku=SDSQXCD-128G-GN6MA)
- Camera: [Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/camera-module-3/), wide angle, plus a [Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/camera-cable/)
- AI accelerator: see [AI accelerator](#ai-accelerator)
- Radar (recommended): [OmniPreSense OPS243-A](https://omnipresense.com/product/ops243-doppler-radar-sensor/)
- Enclosure: see [Enclosure](#enclosure)
- Air quality sensor (optional): [Enviro+](https://www.pishop.us/product/enviro-for-raspberry-pi/) with the [PMS5003 particulate matter sensor](https://www.pishop.us/product/pms5003-particulate-matter-sensor-with-cable/) and a [male-to-female GPIO ribbon cable](https://www.pishop.us/product/male-to-female-gpio-ribbon-cable/)
- Screws: assorted M3 for the boards and enclosure, M2.5×10 mm for the Raspberry Pi

## Computer

The [Raspberry Pi 5](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-5/) with 4 GB of memory runs the standard setup. Choose 8 GB if you plan to add sensors or other applications. Add the [active cooler](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/active-cooler/); it's inexpensive and prevents throttling on hot days.

Warning

The Raspberry Pi 4 and earlier can't supply enough power over USB for the accelerator and the radar together, which causes resets and dropped readings. Some people have run object detection alone on older models.

### Storage

A good microSD card of 32 GB or more holds the system and the database. Both the [Raspberry Pi SD card](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/sd-cards/?variant=sd-64gb) and the [SanDisk Extreme Pro](https://www.westerndigital.com/products/memory-cards/sandisk-extreme-pro-uhs-i-microsd?sku=SDSQXCD-128G-GN6MA) have been tested. An NVMe (M.2) drive is faster and more durable, and some M.2 HATs hold both a drive and a Coral accelerator.

### Power

The Raspberry Pi 5 needs a 27 W supply (5 V at 5 A). A weaker supply, such as an older Raspberry Pi adapter, causes resets and throttling. The device itself draws 6 to 14 W while detecting, and every part is powered from the Raspberry Pi.

- **Mains:** the official [27 W USB-C power supply](https://www.pishop.us/product/raspberry-pi-27w-usb-c-power-supply-black-us/).
- **Power over Ethernet:** a PoE HAT such as the [Waveshare PoE HAT (F)](https://www.waveshare.com/poe-hat-f.htm) or [Waveshare PoE M.2 HAT+](https://www.waveshare.com/PoE-M.2-HAT-Plus.htm), with a PoE+ source such as the [Raspberry Pi PoE+ injector](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/poe-plus-injector/).
- **Battery for about a day:** a portable power station such as a [Jackery Explorer 300](https://www.jackery.com/products/jackery-explorer-300-v2-portable-power-station), with the official power supply plugged into it. A 300 Wh station lasts about a day.

Longer off-grid use: custom battery and solar

**Battery.** Use a 12 V or 24 V [LiFePO₄](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_iron_phosphate_battery) battery and a [buck converter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buck_converter) that steps it down to 5 V at 5 A. Size the battery from the device's draw of about 13 W: a 12 V, 10 Ah battery (120 Wh) lasts about 9 hours, and 24 hours needs 13 × 24 = 312 Wh, a 12 V battery of about 30 Ah.

**Solar.** Add a [photovoltaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaics) panel and a [charge controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge_controller) to the battery setup. Size the panel for the worst month:

1. Look up your daily [solar potential](https://profilesolar.com/countries/US/). Portland, Oregon, gets about 7.15 kWh/day in summer and 1.42 kWh/day in winter per kW of panel.
1. Multiply by the panel size. A 100 W panel in a Portland winter produces about 1.42 × 0.1 = 142 Wh per day.
1. Allow for the controller. A PWM controller passes about 80%, so 142 × 0.8 = 113 Wh per day.
1. Compare with the 312 Wh the device uses per day. A 100 W panel isn't enough; a Portland winter needs about 300 W of panel.

Real output depends on panel angle, cloud, shade from trees, and snow. This setup is a prototype, not a tested product.

## Cameras

The [Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/camera-module-3/) in its wide-angle version is the tested camera. It needs the [Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/camera-cable/), sold separately. The [Raspberry Pi Global Shutter camera](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-global-shutter-camera/) has been tested too, for faster motion or a custom lens, with the same cable. It needs camera stream settings that match its sensor, because the defaults are for Camera Module 3. They're in `/var/lib/go2rtc/go2rtc.yaml`, which every update replaces, so redo them after updating.

The Raspberry Pi 5 has two camera connectors, so it can take two Raspberry Pi cameras. Network cameras also work; see [Frigate's camera recommendations](https://docs.frigate.video/frigate/hardware#cameras). Choose one that streams H.265 (HEVC), which the Raspberry Pi 5 decodes in hardware. H.264 works with software decoding but costs CPU, so keep to one or two such cameras.

## AI accelerator

An AI accelerator runs the object detection model at over 100 frames per second with a few milliseconds per inference, enough for several cameras. Without one, Frigate detects on the CPU, which is slower and misses more objects on a busy road, so an accelerator is recommended for any deployment with a camera.

1. **Recommended:** [Raspberry Pi AI HAT+](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/ai-hat/) with the Hailo-8 or Hailo-8L.
1. **Older:** [Coral USB Accelerator](https://coral.ai/products/accelerator). It has become expensive and hard to find.
1. **Older:** [Coral M.2 Accelerator B+M key](https://coral.ai/products/m2-accelerator-bm/) (not the A+E key) on the [Raspberry Pi M.2 HAT+](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/m2-hat-plus/).

Frigate's [supported detectors](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/object_detectors) lists other options. The installer detects the Coral and Hailo accelerators and configures Frigate for whichever it finds.

## Radar

The [OmniPreSense OPS243-A](https://omnipresense.com/product/ops243-doppler-radar-sensor/) Doppler radar measures speed and direction up to about 100 m away and is certified with the same tests as law-enforcement speed radars. It connects over USB.

## Air quality sensor

The [Enviro+](https://www.pishop.us/product/enviro-for-raspberry-pi/) board with the [PMS5003 particulate matter sensor](https://www.pishop.us/product/pms5003-particulate-matter-sensor-with-cable/) measures gases, particulates, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light. It plugs into the Raspberry Pi's GPIO header through a [male-to-female ribbon cable](https://www.pishop.us/product/male-to-female-gpio-ribbon-cable/), which reaches the sensor's place in the enclosure. [Air quality sensor](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/air-quality/index.md) covers the software.

## Enclosure

- **Print it.** The 3D-printable enclosure is open source at [greendormer/tm-enclosure-3d](https://github.com/greendormer/tm-enclosure-3d), with a parts list.
- **Adapt a junction box.** A waterproof electrical box of about 9 × 7 × 4 inches, such as the [TICONN IP67 ABS enclosure](https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0B87X944Z), holds the parts, the camera, and the radar with some modification.

# Update the software

An update reruns the installer from a newer copy of the repository. Your data and your settings stay; the containers are rebuilt.

## Before you update

- Read the [release notes](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/releases). A release that needs a fresh image says so.
- Download a copy of the database from the [Data export](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/database/#download-the-database) page.
- Make sure the device has an internet connection. The update downloads packages and rebuilds the container images. Rebuilding Frigate's image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which can take about 20 minutes.

## Update

Connect to the device over SSH, then update the clone you installed from and rerun the whole installer:

```
cd traffic-monitor
git pull
bash script/tmsetup.sh
```

Run the whole installer rather than a single tag, because one version's changes can span several components.

Restart when the installer asks. When the services come back, the Node-RED service applies any database schema changes before it opens the database. [Schema versions](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/#schema-versions) describes the copy it saves first.

The installer printed `tm-control migrate: WARNING`

A camera's input `path` in Frigate's configuration reads a stream on port 8554 without a login. If that path points at this device, for example by its IP address, add `{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER}:{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD}@` before the host in Frigate's configuration editor. The [higher-resolution stream](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/#higher-resolution-stream) section shows a complete path. If it points at another device, leave it as it is. To find the warning later:

```
grep 'tm-control migrate: WARNING' ~/tmsetup-*.log
```

A Frigate configuration from a backup may lack the camera stream login. After you restore one, run `bash script/tmsetup.sh -t frigate` to add it.

Port 1883 accepts MQTT connections only from the device itself unless the broker has a login. If a display board, Home Assistant, or another device on your network reads MQTT from this device, give the broker a login and give it to that device; see [Connect from other devices](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#connect-from-other-devices).

Open `http://<device>/` and check the [Monitoring dashboard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/monitoring/index.md) for new counts.

To update several devices from your computer, use the remote form of the installer described in [Install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/#install-from-another-computer).

## What an update changes

An update replaces the container images, service units, Node-RED flows, and the reverse proxy configuration. It keeps your settings files, the database, and Frigate's recordings. With `-f`, it also replaces the settings files with fresh copies from the templates and keeps each old file beside the new one with a timestamp. [What `-f` replaces](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/#what-f-replaces) lists the files.

Use `-f` when a release changes the settings files and you want the new template. Afterwards, turn Frigate's detection back on and redo your settings from the timestamped copies: location and sensors in `config.yml`, and zones in Frigate. [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md) walks through each.

Node-RED flow changes made in the editor on the device are replaced on every update. Commit them to the repository instead; see [Dev environment](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/dev-environment/index.md).

## Update one component

Each installer tag reruns one component, plus anything that has to change with it; see [Tags](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/#tags). For example, after plugging in a radar:

```
bash script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm
```

[Installer options](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/index.md) lists the tags and flags.

# Install the software

The Traffic Monitor runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). One installer script sets up the operating system, detects the radars and the AI accelerator, builds the containers on the device, and reboots when it needs to.

## Prepare the card

1. Open [Raspberry Pi Imager](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/getting-started.html#install-using-imager) on your computer, with the microSD card in a card reader.
1. Choose **Raspberry Pi OS (other) > Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit)**. The full desktop image works but installs software the Traffic Monitor doesn't use.
1. In [OS customization](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/getting-started.html#advanced-options), set a hostname, a username and password, your Wi-Fi network, and turn on SSH. The hostname becomes the device's address on your network: `http://<hostname>.local/`.
1. Write the card, put it in the Raspberry Pi, and power it on. The first boot takes a few minutes.

## Install on the device

The device needs an internet connection during the install. Afterwards it runs offline.

Connect over SSH with the username and hostname you chose:

```
ssh <username>@<hostname>.local
```

Then download the repository and run the installer:

```
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git
git clone https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh
```

The installer asks for your password when it needs administrator rights. A first install takes 30 minutes or more. Building Frigate's container image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which alone takes about 20 minutes with little output, so leave it running.

Near the end, the installer asks to reboot. A first install always needs the reboot, with or without an AI accelerator, because it changes the Raspberry Pi's boot settings for the camera and any accelerator it found. The services start after the reboot. After it, open `http://<hostname>.local/` and continue with [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md).

The installer's flags, such as a different install folder or time zone, are listed in [Installer options](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/index.md).

## Install from another computer

The same script can install or update one or more devices over SSH from a Linux or Mac computer. Each device needs Raspberry Pi OS, a network connection, and an address you can reach.

```
git clone https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -H <address>[,<address>] -l <username> -k -K
```

| Flag | Meaning                                                                           |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-H` | The devices' hostnames or IP addresses, separated by commas                       |
| `-l` | The username you set when imaging the cards. It must be the same on every device. |
| `-k` | Ask for the SSH password                                                          |
| `-K` | Ask for the password for administrator rights. Raspberry Pi OS requires it.       |

Remote devices reboot by themselves when the install needs it.

## Next steps

1. [Choose a site and mount](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/index.md) the device.
1. [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md): turn on detection, adjust the zones, and record the location.
# Deploy

# Choose a site and mount

Deployment covers where the device goes, how it's mounted, and the angle of the camera and radar to the roadway. The zones and location are set afterwards in [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md).

Danger

**Follow the law.** Comply with all applicable laws and local regulations when installing, mounting, and deploying a Traffic Monitor, particularly in public spaces. Unauthorized surveillance can lead to legal consequences and infringe privacy rights. Consult legal professionals or local authorities if you are unsure of the requirements. This guide is for educational purposes; you are responsible for complying with the law and for the consequences of deploying and using the device.

Mount the device only where you have permission, and don't attach it to utility poles without proper authorization.

## Mounting options

Choose a mount that lets you make fine adjustments, because the radar's angle and position need tuning on site.

The open source, 3D-printed [enclosure](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/#enclosure) has several mounting methods built in, depending on the variant:

- 1/4"-20 screw insert on the bottom and back, for camera and trail-camera mounting hardware
- VESA-compatible holes (75 and 100 mm)
- Arca-Swiss-compatible quick-release plate on the bottom, for tripods
- Strap slots on the back, for posts, poles, and trees
- Safety tether hole for a carabiner and strap

Back: VESA holes, 1/4"-20 screw insert, strap slots, and safety tether hole (lower left)

Bottom: Arca-Swiss quick-release plate and 1/4"-20 screw insert

## Temporary deployments

For counts over a few hours, such as an event or a point-in-time study, mount the device at or above head height with an unobstructed view of the roadway. A sturdy tripod and a compact portable power station work well.

On a 16-foot telescoping tripod, counting event participants

Recording manual confirmation counts, with the device on a camera tripod and a portable power station

## Permanent deployments

Warning

**Work safely.** Use proper safety equipment and ladder practice. Make sure the device is securely mounted, all fasteners are tight, the safety tether is in place, and the mount is stable. Failure to do so can cause injury or property damage.

Long-term deployments work anywhere the camera has a good view of the roadway and the radar can be aimed along it: garage roofs, a wood post in a cement-filled bucket, a stone pillar. Keep the device out of reach and clear of anything that might grow or be parked in front of it.

Long-term deployments, with permission, on a private rooftop and a gate entrance

## Best practices

- Mount the device above the roadway and out of reach, about 10 to 12 feet up, for the best view and the least tampering.
- Choose a clear view of the road. Objects are still tracked when they pass briefly behind a tree or lamp post.
- Keep the radar off parking spots and other places where vehicles stop, because stationary vehicles get in the way of its readings.
- The camera detects objects anywhere in its field of view, so frame the whole stretch of road you care about.
- Think about which [zones](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/#3-adjust-the-zones) your use case needs, and whether the view lets you draw them.

### Sample deployments

Quiet road, monitoring downhill movement

Busy business district, nearly head-on movement on a wide road

Busy business district, side-on view focused on a pedestrian and bike crosswalk

Neighborhood greenway, an ideal spot to count bikes, pedestrians, and cars

Greenway mounting spot, facing south

Greenway mounting spot, facing north

### Camera considerations

The camera detects objects anywhere in the frame, so cover the whole area of interest even if the roadway isn't centered. An unobstructed view gives the best results.

Detections can happen anywhere in the camera's field of view

### Radar considerations

The radar has a narrower field of view than the camera and measures speed accurately only at a shallow angle to the direction of travel.

- Aim the device so that traffic moves toward or away from it at **45 degrees or less**. The [OmniPreSense field-of-view calculator](https://omnipresense.com/ops243-field-of-view-calculator/) shows how the angle affects the reading.
- The radar labels movement **inbound** (toward the device) and **outbound** (away from it), and the camera uses the same words. Place the device so those directions make sense for your roadway, for example inbound for downhill traffic.
- To find the radar's coverage, have someone hold the radar outside the case and watch the red and blue LEDs on its front as people and vehicles pass. Where the LEDs blink is where to draw `zone_radar`.

## Next steps

Plug the device in. It starts by itself, and the green LED on the Raspberry Pi shows it has power. Continue with [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md).

# First-time setup

Do these steps once the device is [mounted](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/index.md) and powered on, and again whenever you move it. You need a computer or phone on the same network, and an SSH client for step 4.

As installed, the camera and the first radar are turned on in the Traffic Monitor's settings, but Frigate's object detection is off. Nothing is counted until you turn it on in step 2.

## 1. Open the home page

Open `http://<device>/`, where `<device>` is the hostname you set when imaging the card followed by `.local`, or the device's IP address. [Home page and apps](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/home-page/index.md) explains each link and how to find the address.

## 2. Turn on detection

1. Open **Frigate** from the home page.
1. Go to **Settings > Configuration editor**.
1. Under `cameras: picam_h265: detect:`, change `enabled: false` to `enabled: true`.
1. Choose **Save & Restart**.

When Frigate is back, its live view draws a box around anything that moves past the camera.

## 3. Adjust the zones

The Traffic Monitor looks for four zones with fixed names. Frigate ships with all four drawn for a sample roadway; drag their corners to fit yours.

1. In Frigate, go to **Settings > Camera configuration > Masks / Zones**.
1. Edit each zone in the table below, then save. Frigate restarts.

| Zone           | Draw it over                                                                                                                                            | Used for                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `zone_capture` | The whole roadway you want to count, including sidewalks that are clearly in view                                                                       | Counting. An object is counted only if it passes through this zone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `zone_near`    | The half of `zone_capture` closest to the device                                                                                                        | Direction                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `zone_far`     | The half of `zone_capture` farthest from the device                                                                                                     | Direction. An object that enters `zone_near` and then `zone_far` is moving **outbound**, away from the device; the reverse is **inbound**.                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `zone_radar`   | The part of the road the radar covers accurately, roughly a rectangle from curb to curb in the middle of the frame. Skip it if the device has no radar. | Speed statistics. Any object that enters a zone gets a speed from the radar, but the dashboards' speed statistics use only objects that passed through this zone. [Radar considerations](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/#radar-considerations) shows how to find the radar's coverage. |

The four zones drawn over a residential street

Zones you draw for your own analysis, such as a stop-sign zone or a crosswalk, can have any other name. [Ideas and use cases](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/help-and-faq/use-cases-and-scenarios/index.md) has examples.

## 4. Record the location and sensors

The device records its location with every event, so set it before you collect data. Connect over SSH and open the Traffic Monitor settings file:

```
sudo nano /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml
```

1. Under `deployment`, enter the latitude and longitude from any map service, and the compass direction the camera faces as `n`, `s`, `e`, `w`, `ne`, `nw`, `se`, or `sw`.
1. Under `sensors`, check that the entries match the hardware. A device with the Pi camera and one radar needs no change. A device without a radar needs `enabled: false` under `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00`.

```
deployment:
    lat: 45.5225
    lon: -122.6919
    bearing: n

sensors:
    cameras:
        picam_h265:
            enabled: true
            camera_radar: TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00
    radars:
        TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00:
            enabled: true
```

Save with Ctrl+O and leave nano with Ctrl+X. The Traffic Monitor reads the file again as soon as you save it, so no restart is needed. A change that doesn't take effect usually means a YAML error, such as a wrong indent.

[config.yml settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/index.md) describes every setting in this file, including the optional [ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/index.md) upload.

## 5. Check the counts

Open **Dashboard** from the home page and choose **Monitoring** in the sidebar. [Monitoring](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/monitoring/index.md) shows a count a few seconds after each object passes through `zone_capture`, and speed statistics for objects that also passed through `zone_radar`. Today's counts start at 04:00 local time, so between midnight and 04:00 they're empty.

No counts?

Work down the list:

1. **Frigate shows no boxes around moving objects.** Detection is off (step 2), or the camera is off: in the configuration editor, `cameras: picam_h265:` needs `enabled: true`. If the live view is black, open **Go2RTC Feeds** from the home page to check that the camera itself streams.
1. **Frigate detects objects, but the dashboard stays at zero.** The objects aren't passing through `zone_capture` (step 3), or the camera is off in the Traffic Monitor's settings: `sensors: cameras: picam_h265:` needs `enabled: true`, and the name must match Frigate's camera name. If your edits don't take effect, check the file for a YAML error.
1. **Counts but no speeds.** The radar must be `enabled: true` and named in the camera's `camera_radar`, `zone_radar` must cover the road, and the radar must have been plugged in when the software was installed. If you added it later, rerun `bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm`.
1. **Still nothing.** Look at the logs in [System administration](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/index.md), then ask in the [chat](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/help-and-faq/where-can-i-get-support/index.md).
# Use the device

## description: The device's home page and the apps it links to: dashboards, Frigate, Node-RED, camera feeds, and Cockpit.

# Home page and apps

Open `http://<device>/` in a browser on the same network. `<device>` is the hostname you set when you imaged the card, followed by `.local` (for example `http://tm-01.local/`), or the device's IP address.

The home page links to every app on the device.

| Link                                  | Path          | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Login                          |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Dashboard                             | `/dashboard/` | The Traffic Monitor dashboards: [Monitoring](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/monitoring/index.md), [Movements](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/movements/index.md), and [Data export](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/database/index.md), which opens first. Switch pages in the sidebar.                                                                                                                   | None                           |
| Frigate                               | `/frigate/`   | Object detection: live view, detections with snapshots and clips, zones, masks, and the Frigate settings. See [Tune object detection](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                                              | None                           |
| Legacy Dashboard                      | `/ui/`        | The older dashboard, with the same counts and speed statistics as Monitoring. It's the only dashboard that shows [air quality](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/air-quality/index.md) readings, and the Monitoring dashboard's counts follow its camera and radar selection. Its System Settings tab shows the device's name, time zone, and software versions, and holds the ThingsBoard Backup & Restore section. | None                           |
| Node-RED admin console                | `/nr/`        | The flow editor, for developers. See [Dev environment](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/dev-environment/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | `admin` / `password`           |
| Go2RTC Feeds                          | `/feeds/`     | The camera streams the Pi camera produces, for checking that the camera works. It's for watching only: go2rtc's settings, stream editor, and log pages aren't available here.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | None                           |
| Cockpit-Project system administration | `/system/`    | Services, logs, containers, and a terminal. See [System administration](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Your Raspberry Pi user account |

Finding the device's address

- If you set a hostname in Raspberry Pi Imager, `http://<hostname>.local/` works from most computers and phones on the same network.
- Otherwise, look the device up in your router's list of connected devices, or see [Find the IP address of your Raspberry Pi](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/remote-access.html#ip-address).
- A pre-built unit may host its own Wi-Fi network. Connect to it and use the hostname or the gateway address. Your provider's instructions take precedence.

If the home page doesn't load

The apps accept connections only from the device, so they have no address of their own on your network. Open Cockpit at `http://<device>:9090`, log in with your Raspberry Pi user account, and check the services as described in [System administration](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/index.md). [Network ports](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/network/index.md) lists what the device opens.

# System administration

## Cockpit

Open `http://<device>/system/` and log in with your Raspberry Pi user account. [Cockpit](https://cockpit-project.org/) shows the services and their logs, the Podman containers, system updates, and a terminal, so most administration needs no SSH client.

## Services

The Traffic Monitor runs as systemd services. The app containers run inside one Podman pod. nginx runs on the host network, outside the pod, so the home page stays up when the pod is down.

| Service                    | What it runs                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `traffic-monitor.service`  | The pod that holds Frigate, Node-RED, and Plate Recognizer if installed                                      |
| `frigate.service`          | Frigate, object detection                                                                                    |
| `node-red-tm.service`      | Node-RED: the Traffic Monitor logic, dashboards, database, and MQTT broker                                   |
| `revproxy.service`         | nginx, which serves the home page and the `/dashboard/`, `/frigate/`, and other paths                        |
| `plate-recognizer.service` | The optional [Plate Recognizer](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/plate-recognizer/index.md) add-on |
| `go2rtc_server.service`    | go2rtc, which reads the Pi camera and streams it to Frigate. It runs on the host, not in the pod.            |

Over SSH:

```
sudo systemctl status traffic-monitor.service   # or any service above
sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service      # after editing node-red-tm.env
sudo journalctl -u frigate.service -f           # follow a service's log
sudo podman ps                                  # running containers
```

## When to restart what

| After you                                         | Do this                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Edit Node-RED's `config.yml`                      | Nothing. The Traffic Monitor reads the file again when you save it. If the change doesn't show, check the file for a YAML error.                                                                             |
| Edit `node-red-tm.env`                            | `sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service`. The container reads the file only when it starts.                                                                                                              |
| Change the MQTT broker login in `node-red-tm.env` | `bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm`. A restart isn't enough; [node-red-tm.env settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/environment/index.md) explains why.             |
| Change Frigate's config in its UI                 | Choose **Save & Restart** in Frigate's config editor, or restart `frigate.service`.                                                                                                                          |
| Plug in a radar                                   | Rerun the installer for Node-RED so the radar is passed to the container: `bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm`.                                                                           |
| Add or change an AI accelerator                   | Rerun the installer with `-t detectors -t frigate`, then update Frigate's detector settings. See [Add an accelerator later](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/#add-an-accelerator-later). |
| Move the device to a new site                     | Follow [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md) again: adjust the zones and update the location.                                                                          |

## Where things are

Everything the installer manages lives under `/opt/traffic-monitor/`.

| Path                                    | Contents                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `node-red-tm/config/config.yml`         | Traffic Monitor settings. See [config.yml settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/index.md).                 |
| `node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env`           | Radar ports, database path, MQTT broker. See [node-red-tm.env settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/environment/index.md). |
| `node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite`            | The database. `db/backup/` holds the copy saved before the most recent schema change.                                                           |
| `frigate/config/config.yml`             | Frigate's settings, including zones and masks.                                                                                                  |
| `frigate/storage/`                      | Frigate's snapshots and recordings.                                                                                                             |
| `plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env` | Plate Recognizer credentials, if the add-on is installed.                                                                                       |

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The Data export dashboard: download the database or a JSON export, and add comments for whoever analyzes the data.

# Data export

Open `http://<device>/dashboard/database`, or **Database** in the dashboard's sidebar. This page gets data off the device and lets you leave notes in it.

The Data export page

## Comments

A comment is a timestamped note stored in the `comments` table, for whoever analyzes the data later: a settings change, road work, an event in the area. Give it an effective date and an optional expiry date, the text, and your name; only the name is required. The form also has time fields, but only the dates are kept. Without an effective date, the comment takes effect when you save it. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/#comments) lists the columns.

## Download the database

Downloads the whole database as a compressed archive named `<hostname>_<time>_tmdb.tar.gz`. The page shows the database's size in megabytes. The device first makes a consistent copy of the database, so a large one can take a minute or two before the download starts. The copy needs free space about the size of the database; if there isn't enough, the page says so. A 3 GB file can then take about 5 minutes to compress and several more to download. Cancel also works while the copy is being made: the download stops once the copy is done, and no archive is sent. If a download fails, you see the reason instead of a broken file.

Unpack the archive with `tar -xvzf` on Linux or Mac, or with [7-Zip](https://www.7-zip.org/) on Windows. Inside is `tmdb.sqlite`, which opens in [DB Browser for SQLite](https://sqlitebrowser.org/) or any SQLite library.

## Download JSON

Exports part of the data as JSON files in a compressed archive named `<hostname>_<time>_json.tar.gz`. Choose what to export and a start and end time, which default to the last 7 days:

| Choice                                     | Contents                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Everything                                 | The `events` table, the five radar tables, and the `airquality` table |
| All event types                            | The whole `events` table for the time range                           |
| One object type, such as `car` or `person` | The events of that type                                               |
| Air quality                                | The `airquality` table                                                |
| Radar                                      | The radar tables                                                      |

The files are plain JSON, readable in any text editor or loaded straight into a notebook.

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The Monitoring dashboard: today's counts, car speed statistics, hourly and daily charts, and the latest events with their radar readings.

# Monitoring

Open `http://<device>/dashboard/monitoring`, or open **Dashboard** from the home page and choose **Monitoring** in the sidebar. Monitoring shows the counts and speed statistics for one camera and one radar at a time.

The Monitoring page, numbered as in the list below

1. **Sensor selection.** A radar and a camera picker, listing every sensor in [config.yml](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/#sensorscameras), enabled or not. The counts and statistics on this page follow the camera and radar selected on the legacy dashboard at `http://<device>/ui/`, not the selection here. On a device with one camera and one radar, they're the same.

1. **Car speed statistics** for the current day, which starts at 04:00 local time. They cover `car` events that passed through both `zone_capture` and `zone_radar` and got a speed from the radar. Speeds are absolute values, so inbound and outbound are pooled, and every value is rounded to a whole number.

   The percentiles come from sorting the day's cars by speed and splitting them into 20 groups of equal size, so they're approximate. With few cars, some stay empty: the 25th percentile needs 5 cars, the median 10, the 75th percentile and `iqr_upper` 15, and the 85th percentile 17.

   | Statistic                                          | Meaning                                                                                                                                                     |
   | -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   | `count`                                            | Cars with a speed                                                                                                                                           |
   | `mean_speed`                                       | Average speed                                                                                                                                               |
   | `p25_speed`, `p50_speed`, `p75_speed`, `p85_speed` | 25th, 50th (median), 75th, and 85th [percentile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percentile) speeds. The 85th percentile is the usual basis for speed limits. |
   | `max_speed`                                        | Fastest car                                                                                                                                                 |
   | `count_over_25`                                    | Cars faster than 25, in the radar's units                                                                                                                   |
   | `iqr_upper`                                        | The outlier line: `p75_speed` plus 1.5 times the [interquartile range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interquartile_range)                                   |
   | `iqr_upper_freq`                                   | Cars faster than `iqr_upper`, the outliers                                                                                                                  |

1. **Today's counts** by object type for events that passed through `zone_capture`. The day starts at 04:00 local time, so from midnight until 04:00 these counts and the speed statistics are empty. Objects that pass in those hours are left out of the day's counts, but they appear in the hourly and daily charts.

1. **Hourly counts** by object type for the last 36 hours, for events that passed through `zone_capture`.

1. **Daily counts** by object type for the last 10 calendar days, for events that passed through `zone_capture`.

1. **Latest observations.** The 21 most recent events from any camera that passed through `zone_radar`, newest first, including events without a speed. Each card shows Frigate's thumbnail of the object, the direction, the speed, and the radar's raw readings from the start of the event to its end: how many there were ("radar hits"), the range of their magnitudes and speeds, and two charts, **Radar Magnitude** and **Radar Speed**. The charts show whether the readings came from one object or from several at once. They're the raw readings, not the ones the speed was worked out from. The list is kept in memory, so it empties when Node-RED restarts.

Counts and statistics come from the `events` table; see [Events](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/index.md). The same counts are published over MQTT on `tm/events`; see [MQTT and ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#tmevents).

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The Movements dashboard: counts of objects by the sequence of zones they passed through, for checking against manual counts.

# Movements

Open `http://<device>/dashboard/movements`. Movements counts objects by the path they took through your zones, which is how you check the device against a manual count or confirm that the zones capture what you want.

Movements come from the `entered_zones` of each [event](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/index.md), so they depend on how the [zones](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/#3-adjust-the-zones) are drawn.

The Movements page

1. **Zones.** Tick the zones to include. The four standard `zone_*` zones are unticked by default, so that zones you drew for your own analysis stand out.
1. **Intermediate zones.** Choose **Show intermediate zones** to count each full sequence of zones separately, or **Show just initial & final zones** to group by where an object entered and where it left.
1. **Time range.** Start and end times; the last 7 days by default. In time zones east of UTC, or with a half-hour offset, the page shows no counts for any range.
1. **Counts** by object type for each zone sequence that matches.

## Example: a complex intersection

An intersection with many zones has dozens of possible movements. Each turn or crossing becomes its own row, which you can compare with a manual count sheet.

Twelve zones drawn on a busy five-way intersection

Manual confirmation counts; the left sheet matches the zones above

# Tune object detection

[Frigate](https://frigate.video/) does the object detection. How well it works depends on the mounting height and angle, the camera, and the weather, so expect to adjust it for each site. The Traffic Monitor is not affiliated with the Frigate project.

The Traffic Monitor's [default Frigate config](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/frigate/config/config.yml.j2) is tuned for roadways seen from an oblique angle, with a side view of objects as they pass. Everything in it can be changed in Frigate's own UI, at **Settings > Configuration editor**. Frigate's [configuration reference](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/) explains every setting.

## See what Frigate sees

Go to **Settings > Debug** to watch detections live with their scores, and the motion regions Frigate is checking. **Explore** lists past detections with their snapshots, which is the quickest way to find missed bikes or a tree that's being called a person.

The debug view shows how detection is performing

## Object filters

Frigate tracks `bicycle`, `person`, `car`, `bus`, `motorcycle`, and `dog` by default. Each object type has two scores in the `objects: filters:` section of the config:

- `min_score` is the score needed to start tracking an object.
- `threshold` is the average score an object needs, over the time it's tracked, to count as a real detection.

The defaults set `bicycle` low, so most kinds of bike are detected, and `motorcycle` high, so a large e-bike isn't called a motorcycle. If you see false positives for a type, raise its `threshold`; if you miss objects, lower it. Frigate's [object filters](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/object_filters/#object-scores) page describes these and the size and shape filters.

## Masks

Go to **Settings > Camera configuration > Masks / Zones**.

- A **motion mask** stops motion in an area, such as swaying branches or a timestamp overlay, from triggering detection.
- An **object mask** ignores detections of one object type in an area, such as a parked car that's detected every time the light changes.

Warning

Use masks sparingly. Over-masking makes objects harder to track. A motion mask isn't the tool for cutting false positives; adjust the object filters first.

Frigate's [masks](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/masks) page has the details.

## Higher-resolution stream

The Pi camera is set up to produce two streams. Frigate uses `picam_h265_detect` at 1536×864 by default, which gives the best balance of detail and load. A second stream, `picam_h265_detect_hr`, runs at 2304×1296 for cases where objects are small in the frame.

To switch, change two things in the configuration editor under `cameras: picam_h265:`: the input `path` to `rtsp://{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER}:{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD}@host.containers.internal:8554/picam_h265_detect_hr`, and `detect: width: 2304` with `height: 1296`. Frigate fills in the `{…}` values from `frigate.env`. Then redraw the [zones](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/#3-adjust-the-zones) for the new frame size. The higher resolution costs CPU and may lower the frame rate on a busy road.

## Recordings and snapshots

By default, Frigate keeps a cropped snapshot of each detection and a recording of each alert and detection for about an hour, so you can check what was detected. The `record:` and `snapshots:` sections control this: set `enabled: false` to keep nothing, or raise `retain: days` to keep more. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/index.md) describes what the device stores.

Frigate can also publish a cropped snapshot of each detected object on the device's [MQTT broker](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#mqtt). The Traffic Monitor doesn't use these snapshots, so new installs turn them off with `mqtt: enabled: false` under `cameras: picam_h265:`. On an older install, add those lines in the configuration editor. Frigate keeps publishing the events the Traffic Monitor counts.

```
cameras:
  picam_h265:
    mqtt:
      enabled: false
```

## Better models

[Frigate+](https://docs.frigate.video/plus/) offers paid models fine-tuned on your own snapshots, which can raise accuracy for a difficult site.
# Reference

# config.yml settings

The Traffic Monitor's own settings live in `/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml` on the device. The installer writes it from [this template](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/node-red-tm/config/config.yml.j2) on the first install and leaves it alone afterwards, unless you run the installer with `-f`.

The Traffic Monitor reads the file again whenever you save it, so changes take effect without a restart. If the file has a YAML error, it keeps the previous settings until the service restarts, and after a restart it has no settings at all until you fix the file.

Keep the four top-level sections (`thingsboard`, `deployment`, `sensors`, `time`) in the file. The Default column below shows the values the template writes. A setting that's missing from the file behaves differently in a few cases:

- A camera or radar without `enabled` is off.
- A radar without `opt_api_commands_array` gets no extra commands.
- ThingsBoard without `host` stays off.
- A `deployment` without `lat` or `lon` isn't recorded, so leave the keys in place even when they're empty.
- A camera whose `camera_radar` names a radar that isn't in the file records no events. On a device without a radar, remove `camera_radar` or keep the radar's entry with `enabled: false`.

## thingsboard

Uploads events, readings, and device telemetry to a [ThingsBoard](https://thingsboard.io/) server. See [MQTT and ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/index.md).

| Setting        | Type              | Default                         | Meaning                                                                         |
| -------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`      | `true` or `false` | `false`                         | Turn the upload on.                                                             |
| `host`         | text              | `tb.server.com` (a placeholder) | The server's hostname, without protocol or port. Required when enabled.         |
| `protocol`     | `http` or `https` | `https`                         | How to reach the server.                                                        |
| `port`         | number            | none                            | Set it only if the server isn't on the standard port for the protocol.          |
| `access_token` | text              | empty                           | The device's access token from ThingsBoard. This is the one secret in the file. |

## deployment

Where the device is. Every event and reading is stored with a deployment id that points at these values, so set them before you collect data and update them when you move the device.

| Setting   | Type                                          | Default | Meaning                                                    |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `lat`     | decimal degrees, such as `45.5225`            | empty   | Latitude. Four decimal places give address-level accuracy. |
| `lon`     | decimal degrees, such as `-122.6919`          | empty   | Longitude.                                                 |
| `bearing` | `n`, `s`, `e`, `w`, `ne`, `nw`, `se`, or `sw` | empty   | The compass direction the camera and radar face.           |

A `deployment:` block with the same three settings under any sensor overrides these for that sensor, for a device whose cameras face different ways.

## sensors.cameras

One entry per camera, named exactly as the camera is named in Frigate. The default camera is `picam_h265`. Events from a camera that isn't listed here, or is disabled, are ignored.

| Setting            | Type                               | Default                   | Meaning                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`          | `true` or `false`                  | `true` for `picam_h265`   | Record this camera's events. Frigate keeps running either way.                                                                    |
| `camera_radar`     | a radar name from `sensors.radars` | `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00` | The radar that supplies speeds for this camera. One radar can serve several cameras. Leave it out on a device without a radar.    |
| `plate_recognizer` | `true` or `false`                  | `false`                   | Send this camera's events to the [Plate Recognizer](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/plate-recognizer/index.md) add-on. |
| `deployment`       | block                              | inherited                 | Per-camera `lat`, `lon`, and `bearing`.                                                                                           |

## sensors.radars

One entry per radar. A radar's name is the name of the variable that holds its serial port in [node-red-tm.env](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/environment/index.md), `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00` through `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_03`.

| Setting                  | Type                     | Default                              | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`                | `true` or `false`        | `true` for `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00` | Read this radar. Set it to `false` on a device without a radar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `opt_api_commands_array` | a JSON array in a string | `'["^/+0.00\n", "^/-0.00\n"]'`       | Extra [OPS243 API](https://omnipresense.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/AN-010-Y_API_Interface.pdf) commands sent to the radar when the service starts and whenever you save this file, after the Traffic Monitor's own setup commands. The default sets the cosine correction to 0 degrees in both directions. |
| `deployment`             | block                    | inherited                            | Per-radar `lat`, `lon`, and `bearing`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

## sensors.airquality_monitors

One entry per [air quality sensor](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/air-quality/index.md), named as the middle part of the topic the sensor publishes to: `aq/<name>/readings`.

| Setting               | Type              | Default    | Meaning                                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ----------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`             | `true` or `false` | `false`    | Record this sensor's readings. Readings from a sensor that isn't enabled are dropped.   |
| `mqtt_topic_incoming` | text              | `readings` | Present in the template but not used. The device subscribes to every topic under `aq/`. |

## time

| Setting    | Type                                                                               | Default                                                              | Meaning                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `timezone` | a [tz database name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) | the installer's `-z` value, `America/Los_Angeles` unless you set one | Present in the template but not used. The dashboards and the 04:00 daily reset use the device's time zone, which the installer's `-z` sets. |
| `npt_set`  | `true` or `false`                                                                  | `true`                                                               | Present in the template but not used.                                                                                                       |

## addons.plate_recognizer

Only needed with the [Plate Recognizer](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/plate-recognizer/index.md) add-on. The section isn't in the template; add it.

| Setting | Type | Default | Meaning                                                                 |
| ------- | ---- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `token` | text | none    | Your Plate Recognizer API token. Plates aren't read until this is set.  |
| `url`   | URL  | none    | The add-on's address inside the device, `http://plate-recognizer:8080`. |

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The variables in node-red-tm.env: radar serial ports, database path, MQTT broker, and the values the installer fills in.

# node-red-tm.env settings

`/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env` holds the environment the Node-RED container starts with. The installer writes it from [this template](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env.j2) on the first install and leaves it alone afterwards, unless you run the installer with `-f`. Most devices never need it edited.

After editing it, restart the service:

```
sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service
```

After changing the MQTT broker login

A restart or reboot isn't enough after you change `TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME` or `TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD`. Run the installer instead, so Frigate gets the same login and port 1883 opens or closes to match:

```
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm
```

Otherwise the broker refuses Frigate's connection, and no events are recorded.
